A smart brain for intelligent machines

Embed your intelligence. Connect everything. Explore freely.

Edgeberry is a highly adaptable, open source computer platform that lets you embed your intelligence iteratively into every layer of your smart, connected product — allowing you to explore every corner of your idea, deploy with confidence and easily co-create to evolve the concept.

Embed your intelligence with Edgeberry. Focus on what matters. Iterate to perfection.

An edge computer you can open, change, and keep running.

The application runs on the machine itself. Sensors, control loop and logic in one box, working whether or not there is a network — a connection is something it uses, not something it needs.

Open source here means the object, not a firmware repository. Enclosure, boards, software and SDK are each published under their own licence: CERN-OHL-W, GPL-3, MIT. Print a replacement shell, cut a new cartridge, fork the software, or have a hundred made — without asking anyone, including us.

95 × 27 × 97 mm · Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W · Debian · OSHWA certified BE000020

Powered by Raspberry Pi

Choosing the Pi buys far more than a processor. Kernel support that already works, a package for nearly everything, and an answer to almost any question already written down by someone who hit it first. One image runs across the whole range, so you can develop on a Pi 5 and write the same card to a Zero. And hardware evolution becomes the Foundation's job rather than ours — the Zero 2 W is in production to at least 2030, with pin-compatible alternatives in the same footprint if it ever needs them.

What the carrier adds is the part a Pi on a desk never needs: 12–24 V industrial input brought down to clean 5 V, an identity chip so every unit knows which one it is, a status LED, a button and a buzzer for when there is no screen, and the 32-pin cartridge interface.

Carrier 92.5 × 90 mm · Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W · Raspberry Pi OS

Every application needs its own hardware.

Sooner or later an idea needs a connector nobody sells, a driver for one specific motor, or a sensor at the end of a cable. That is where projects stall — not the software, not the enclosure, but the one board that has to exist and doesn't.

A cartridge is that board, and most of it is already decided. The KiCad template carries the outline, the mounting, the 32-pin interface and the faceplate envelope, so the only part you design is the part only you know about. Swap the cartridge and the device becomes a different instrument, with the compute, the enclosure and the software untouched.

49.8 × 63.2 mm · 32-pin interface · 95 × 27 mm faceplate · template on GitHub

Build it into anything.

You decide where the device sits in your machine, and you print the piece that puts it there. A dovetail rail runs down each side of the enclosure, and anything that slides onto it holds the device.

A foot to screw to a panel, a clip, a bracket shaped to your own frame — each prints as a single part. Two exist so far. The rest is up to whoever needs them.

Dovetail rail both sides · 92.7 mm long · mounts print in one piece

Make it yours.

The device lives in the technical space of your machine — a cabinet, a panel, a bay. The people who open that panel are your people, and a unit in your colour carrying your logo is quicker to recognise, easier to keep track of, and unmistakably part of your system.

Choose the filament for the shell and both faceplates, then drop your logo into the recessed label on the top face. Every unit is printed to order, so the colour is a choice rather than a surcharge. Take the label away as a print-ready SVG with its cut contour, or have the devices built already wearing it.

Bambu Lab PETG · 85 × 25 mm matt label · 0.25 mm recess · SVG export with cut contour

Seamlessly connected.

You write your application with the Edgeberry SDK, in Node.js or Python, and the hardware arrives as functions. Read a sensor, drive an output, publish an event. No protocol code, no drivers, nothing about buses.

The Device Hub carries it from there. Every device has an identity, a group and a state, so your server-side code can invoke a method on one or subscribe to what it sends as though it were any other API. Node-RED sits on top of that for anyone who would rather wire a flow than write one.

SDK for Node.js and Python · Device Hub · MQTT · Node-RED optional
